components.note: 穴 (a cave/hole) — 空 relates to an empty hollow space.
工 (gōng) gives a hint of the sound — 空 is pronounced kōng, a connection that has drifted over time.
门 (door/gate) — 间 pictures light passing through an entryway.
日 (sun) — sunlight shining through a gap in a doorway gave 间 its meaning of a space 'in between,' as in 中间 (in the middle) or 时间 (time, the space between moments).

example.pinyin: Zhège fángjiān de kōngjiān bú dà.
example.english: This room doesn't have much space.
example.fact: 间 is pictured as 门 (a door/gate) with 日 (the sun) — literally sunlight slipping through a doorway — which supplies the "gap, in-between" image that 空间 pairs with 空 ("empty") to build "space"; the same 间 carries that gap sense into 中间 ("in the middle") and 时间 ("time").

components.note: 扌 (hand) does the action.
斤 (axe) — chopping and snapping something in two gives 折 its meaning 'to break, to bend.'
石 (stone) — 磨 names a millstone, or the act of grinding with one.
麻 (má) shares the initial m- and tone with mó, though the rhyme has drifted slightly from á to ó.

example.pinyin: Bìngtòng zhémó le tā hǎojǐ nián.
example.english: The illness tormented him for several years.
example.fact: 折 (from 扌 "hand" plus 斤 "axe" — literally "to snap in two by hand") and 磨 (from 石 "stone," "to grind with a millstone") combine into a vivid image of being broken and ground down, which fits both the physical and the psychological senses 折磨 carries today.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — with strokes above depicting a tongue sticking out — the image of speaking, the source of 言's meaning 'speech, words, language.'

example.pinyin: Tā bú zài, wǒ gěi tā liúyán le.
example.english: He's not in, so I left him a message.
example.fact: 留言 is transparently "words (言) left behind (留)" — a pre-digital word that absorbed new technology wholesale rather than being replaced, so it now covers a scribbled note, a 语音留言 (voicemail), and a comment left on a website alike.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.
今 (now, the present) — represents what is currently on one's mind.
心 (heart/mind) — keeping the present moment in mind gave 念 its meaning 'to think of, to read aloud, to study.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xiǎngniàn jiālǐ de wèidao.
example.english: I really miss the taste of home.
example.fact: 念 is built from 今 ("now, the present") over 心 ("heart/mind") — literally "what's presently on the heart." Paired with 想 ("to think of"), 想念 leans more wistful and literary than bare 想 alone, which can express a lighter, more casual "miss" (想你 vs. the more heartfelt 想念你).

components.note: 口 (mouth) — with strokes above depicting a tongue sticking out — the image of speaking, the source of 言's meaning 'speech, words, language.'

example.hanzi: 对我而言,健康比金钱更重要。
example.pinyin: Duì wǒ éryán, jiànkāng bǐ jīnqián gèng zhòngyào.
example.english: As far as I'm concerned, health matters more than money.
example.fact: 而言 almost never stands alone — it lives inside the fixed frame "对 X 而言" ("as far as X is concerned"), a more formal, written-register alternative to the everyday "对 X 来说"; learners rarely need it outside that one frame.

components.note: 尢 (yóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 尤's reading yóu.

example.hanzi: 我喜欢水果,尤其是芒果。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuan shuǐguǒ, yóuqí shì mángguǒ.
example.english: I like fruit, especially mangoes.
example.fact: 尤其 is almost always followed by 是 (尤其是, "especially [is]") when it singles out one example from a larger category — dropping the 是 is grammatical but noticeably less common in natural speech.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.
马 (horse) — 验 originally related to examining or testing horses, later extended to 'to test, examine, verify'
佥 (qiān) gives a loose sound connection to 验's reading yàn

example.hanzi: 他在这个行业有十年的经验。
example.pinyin: Tā zài zhège hángyè yǒu shí nián de jīngyàn.
example.english: He has ten years of experience in this industry.
example.fact: 经验 names practical experience built up by doing something over time (十年经验, "ten years' experience"), while its near-cousin 体验 is the more subjective, momentary experience of undergoing something, like a ride or an emotion — a distinction English's single word "experience" collapses.

components.note: 皿 (dish, container) — a box is a kind of container.
合 (hé) gives the sound — an exact match for 盒.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 她把照片放进一个盒子里。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ zhàopiàn fàng jìn yí gè hézi lǐ.
example.english: She put the photos into a box.
example.fact: 盒 is built from 皿 ("dish, container") under the phonetic 合 (hé, which itself means "to close, to fit together") — a box is, after all, a container that closes, so the phonetic half happens to carry a scrap of meaning too.

components.note: A pictograph of an ancient forked weapon, such as a club or shield-tipped spear — the tool image later extended to 干's meanings 'to do, to work' and, in another reading, 'dry.'
木 (wood) — 杯 names a cup, originally carved from wood.
不 (bù) shares the initial b- with bēi, though the rhyme has drifted from ù to ēi over time.

example.hanzi: 大家举起杯子,喊道:“干杯!”
example.pinyin: Dàjiā jǔqǐ bēizi, hǎndào: “Gānbēi!”
example.english: Everyone raised their glasses and shouted, "Cheers!"
example.fact: 干杯 literally means "dry cup" (干 "dry" + 杯 "cup") — the toast's implicit instruction is to empty the glass entirely, the same logic behind the English "bottoms up," so the literal and idiomatic senses line up almost exactly.

meanings: way of looking at a thing

components.note: 手 (hand) — depicts a hand raised above the eyes.
目 (eye) — shielding the eyes with a hand to look into the distance gave 看 its meaning 'to look, to see.'
氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.hanzi: 每个人对这件事都有不同的看法。
example.pinyin: Měi gè rén duì zhè jiàn shì dōu yǒu bùtóng de kànfǎ.
example.english: Everyone has a different view on this matter.
example.fact: 看法 literally means "a way (法) of looking (看)" — one of several Chinese abstract nouns for "opinion" built directly on a verb of perception, the same pattern behind 想法 ("way of thinking," idea) and 说法 ("way of saying," account/version).

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
⺼ (flesh/body) — 脑 refers to the brain, a part of the body

example.hanzi: 睡眠对大脑健康很重要。
example.pinyin: Shuìmián duì dànǎo jiànkāng hěn zhòngyào.
example.english: Sleep is very important for brain health.
example.fact: 大脑 technically names the cerebrum specifically, as distinct from 小脑 (the cerebellum) and 脑干 (the brainstem) — but in everyday speech it is used loosely for "the brain" as a whole, the way English "brain" glosses over the same anatomical distinction.

components.note: 罒 (a net) — the law closing in around wrongdoing
非 (wrong) — the wrongdoing itself, caught in the net
犭 (dog) — 犯 originally related to a dog attacking, later extended to any act of violation
㔾 (jié) gives a sound distantly related to 犯's reading fàn, having drifted apart over time

example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zhuāzhù le nàge zuìfàn.
example.english: The police caught the criminal.
example.fact: 罪 (from 罒 "net" over 非 "wrong") pictures wrongdoing caught in a net, and 犯 (from 犭, evoking an attacking animal) names the act of violating a rule — 罪犯 stacks "the crime" and "the violator" together into a single word for the person, not the act.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 从这里到车站不到十分钟。
example.pinyin: Cóng zhèlǐ dào chēzhàn búdào shí fēnzhōng.
example.english: It's less than ten minutes from here to the station.
example.fact: 不到 attaches to a number or quantity to mean "less than, not quite reaching" (不到十分钟, "less than ten minutes") — literally 不 ("not") plus the verb 到 ("to arrive/reach"), a compact way to state an upper bound without a separate word like English "less than."

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 问 relates to speaking, specifically asking a question.
门 (mén) gives a hint of the sound — 问 is pronounced wèn, related but the tone and vowel have shifted.
口 (mouth) — 问 relates to speaking, specifically asking a question.
门 (mén) gives a hint of the sound — 问 is pronounced wèn, related but the tone and vowel have shifted.

example.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ qù wènwen lǎoshī.
example.english: You can go ask the teacher about it.
example.fact: 问问 is simply 问 ("to ask") reduplicated, a common Mandarin device that softens a one-syllable verb into something brief or casual — the same pattern behind 看看 ("take a quick look") and 想想 ("think it over"). It is more a live grammatical process than a fixed dictionary word, which is why standard dictionaries often skip giving it its own entry.

components.note: A pictograph of an ancient forked weapon, such as a club or shield-tipped spear — the tool image later extended to 干's meanings 'to do, to work' and, in another reading, 'dry.'
扌 (hand) — 掉 relates to dropping something from the hand.
卓 (zhuó) reflects an older phonetic connection that has faded in the modern pronunciation diào.

example.hanzi: 我们得想办法干掉这个对手。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen děi xiǎng bànfǎ gàndiào zhège duìshǒu.
example.english: We need to find a way to get rid of this rival.
example.fact: 干掉 pairs the colloquial, all-purpose 干 ("to do," the same 干 in slangy 干什么, "what are you doing") with 掉 used as an "away/off" verb complement, the same role it plays in 扔掉 ("throw away") and 卖掉 ("sell off") — together they read almost like the English slang "do away with."

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 指 relates to using the hand, specifically the fingers.
旨 (an aim, purpose) — combined with 扌 (hand), 指 came to mean 'finger' and 'to point,' aiming the hand at something.
扌 (hand) — 控 relates to controlling or restraining something by hand
空 (kōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 控's reading kòng

example.pinyin: Tā bèi zhǐkòng tōuqiè.
example.english: He was accused of theft.
example.fact: 指控 sits at the formal, legal end of Chinese's "accuse" vocabulary — closer to a courtroom "to charge, to indict" than the everyday 怪 ("to blame") — so it shows up heavily in news and legal reporting rather than casual conversation.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 星 relates to bright heavenly bodies like the sun and stars
生 (shēng) gives a sound close to 星's reading xīng
王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — 球 originally referred to a round piece of jade, extended to mean 'ball, sphere'
求 (qiú) gives the sound — 球 is also pronounced qiú, an exact match

example.hanzi: 地球是一个美丽的星球。
example.pinyin: Dìqiú shì yí gè měilì de xīngqiú.
example.english: Earth is a beautiful celestial body.
example.fact: 星球 combines 星 ("star," any bright point in the sky) with 球 ("ball, sphere") to describe any round heavenly body in general — planets, moons, and stars alike — while 行星 is reserved specifically for "planet," a distinction easy to blur when translating casually from English.

components.note: 录 traditionally depicted a hand-held tool used for carving or writing records — the image behind its meaning 'to record, to write down.'
亻 (person) — relates to 像's meaning 'to resemble, be like; image, portrait,' comparing one person or thing to another.
象 (xiàng) gives the sound — 像 is also pronounced xiàng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen gěi hūnlǐ lùxiàng le.
example.english: We recorded a video of the wedding.
example.fact: 录像 literally means "to record (录) an image (像)" — coined for videotape technology, it has stuck around in everyday Mandarin even in the smartphone era, sitting alongside the newer, more casual 拍视频 ("to shoot a video") as an older but still standard way to talk about recording video.

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 程 originally named a unit for measuring grain, extended to 'process, journey, degree.'
呈 (chéng) gives the sound — 程 is also pronounced chéng, an exact match.
广 (a wide building) — 序 relates to arrangement, as in the ordered layout of a hall.
予 (yǔ) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though it has diverged from the modern reading xù.

example.hanzi: 这是一个新的电脑程序。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí gè xīn de diànnǎo chéngxù.
example.english: This is a new computer program.
example.fact: 程序 meant "sequence, order, procedure" long before computers existed — a bureaucratic and legal term for following the correct steps, as in 法律程序 ("legal procedure") — and simply extended naturally to name a piece of software once Chinese needed a word for "the ordered sequence of instructions a computer follows."

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.
扌 (hand) — 报 relates to taking action against someone.
卩 (a kneeling or bound person) — handling a wrongdoer and announcing the judgment gave 报 its meaning 'to report' or 'to announce.'

example.pinyin: Zhè fèn qíngbào fēicháng zhòngyào.
example.english: This piece of intelligence is extremely important.
example.fact: 情报 leans toward the "intelligence" sense of English "information" — secret, strategic, or military data gathered on purpose — which is why it's the standard word in spy fiction and espionage news (情报机构, "intelligence agency") rather than a synonym for the neutral 信息 or 消息.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.
纟 (thread) — 绪 originally meant the end of a thread, extending to 'clue, beginnings.'
者 (zhě) gives a sound distantly related to xù's reading, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān qíngxù bú tài hǎo.
example.english: He's not in a great mood today.
example.fact: 情绪 technically covers the whole range of emotional states, but in casual speech it's overwhelmingly used to flag something negative (闹情绪, "to sulk"; 情绪化, "moody, emotionally volatile") — similar to how English "emotional" often implies "upset" even though it just means "having emotions."

components.note: 牛 (ox/cattle) — cattle were among the earliest and most valuable kinds of property, connecting 物 to the general idea of 'object' or 'thing.'
勿 (wù) gives the sound — 物 is also pronounced wù, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 孩子害怕床底下有怪物。
example.pinyin: Háizi hàipà chuáng dǐxia yǒu guàiwu.
example.english: The child is afraid there's a monster under the bed.
example.fact: 怪 alone already means "strange, odd," and 物 means "thing, creature" — 怪物 builds "monster" the plain way, as "a strange creature," and can extend loosely to an eccentric or unconventional person, much like English can call an odd genius "a bit of a monster" affectionately.

components.note: 刂 (a knife) — 创 relates to cutting or wounding, extended to mean 'to start, to create,' as a fresh cut marks a new beginning
仓 (cāng) gives a loose sound connection to 创's reading chuàng
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 造's meaning 'to make, build,' an action carried through to completion.
告 (gào) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zào.

example.hanzi: 他们创造了一个新的记录。
example.pinyin: Tāmen chuàngzào le yí gè xīn de jìlù.
example.english: They created a new record.
example.fact: 创造 emphasizes bringing something genuinely new into existence — an invention, a record, a work of art — while its near-synonym 制造 ("to manufacture") is reserved for producing something already known, like a factory turning out identical products; mixing the two up is a common learner slip.

components.note: 乂 depicts crossed strokes suggesting a cutting action.
木 (wood) here represents a wooden stake — giving 杀 its meaning 'to kill.'

example.hanzi: 凶手杀害了三名受害者。
example.pinyin: Xiōngshǒu shāhài le sān míng shòuhàizhě.
example.english: The murderer killed three victims.
example.fact: 杀害 is the formal, written-register word for unlawful killing used in news and legal contexts — plain 杀 alone is more neutral and can describe killing in general, including animals or killing in fiction and games, while 杀害 specifically frames the act as a crime against a person.

components.note: 冂 (an enclosure or doorway) — 内 pictures the space one enters.
人 (person) — a person entering an enclosure gave 内 its meaning 'inside' or 'within.'
心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.

example.hanzi: 她表面平静,内心却很紧张。
example.pinyin: Tā biǎomiàn píngjìng, nèixīn què hěn jǐnzhāng.
example.english: She looked calm on the outside, but inside she was very nervous.
example.fact: 内心 stacks "inside" (内) directly onto "heart" (心) to name one's inner emotional world, often set up in deliberate contrast with 表面 ("surface, outward appearance") — the pattern 表面...内心却... ("outwardly... but inwardly...") is a common way to describe a gap between how someone looks and how they actually feel.

components.note: 日 here pictures a person's head.
共 pictures two hands; together with the shape below, they depict a violent struggle, giving 暴 its meaning 'violent, sudden.'
力 depicts the blade of a plow — since plowing fields took great physical effort, the shape came to represent strength or power.

example.hanzi: 电视上有太多暴力的画面。
example.pinyin: Diànshì shàng yǒu tài duō bàolì de huàmiàn.
example.english: There's too much violent imagery on TV.
example.fact: 暴 alone already means "sudden, violent, fierce," as in 暴雨 ("violent rainstorm") and 暴风 ("violent windstorm") — 暴力 narrows that general sense specifically to violence done to people, adding 力 ("force") to make the meaning concrete and physical.

components.note: 土 (here representing a person swinging their arms, not its usual meaning 'earth') — depicts someone in motion.
止 (a foot) — combined with the moving figure above, 走 shows a person walking or running.
廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'

example.pinyin: Tā shēngqì de shuō: “Nǐ zǒukāi!”
example.english: He said angrily, "Go away!"
example.fact: 走开 as a bare command (走开!, "go away!") sounds sharp and even rude in Mandarin — for a neutral, polite way to ask someone to move aside, speakers reach instead for 让一下 or 借过, so 走开 is one to use carefully depending on tone and relationship.

components.note: 攵 (an action) — ties to 故's sense of a cause or reason behind an action
古 (gǔ) gives a sound close to 故's reading gù

example.hanzi: 昨天路上发生了一起交通事故。
example.pinyin: Zuótiān lù shàng fāshēng le yì qǐ jiāotōng shìgù.
example.english: A traffic accident happened on the road yesterday.
example.fact: 事故 pairs the general 事 ("matter, affair") with 故 ("cause, reason") to name an unplanned "incident with a cause." It's reserved for something unfortunate and usually unintentional (交通事故, "traffic accident"), unlike the neutral 事情 ("matter, affair"), which carries no accident or mishap connotation at all.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 艺 originally related to planting and cultivating skillfully
乙 (yǐ) gives a sound distantly related to 艺's reading yì, having drifted apart over time

example.pinyin: Tā duì yìshù hěn gǎn xìngqù.
example.english: She's very interested in art.
example.fact: 术 on its own means "technique, skill, method," as in 技术 ("technology/skill") and 手术 ("surgery") — 艺术 builds "art" by combining it with 艺 ("skill, craft"), framing art at its root as a cultivated technical skill rather than pure inspiration, a rather different emphasis from the Western Romantic idea of the unteachable "artistic genius."

components.note: 氵 (water) — relates to 满's meaning 'full,' water filling to the brim.
㒼 (mán) gives a sound hint — 满 is pronounced mǎn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.

example.pinyin: Gùkè duì fúwù hěn mǎnyì.
example.english: The customer is very satisfied with the service.
example.fact: 满 alone means "full" — a cup filled to the brim — and 意 means "intention, wish" — 满意 combines them into something not unlike "one's wishes fully met," an image close to the English idiom of one's "cup being full" when deeply satisfied.

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
夕 (evening/night), doubled — two nights stacked together suggested the idea of accumulation, giving 多 its meaning of 'many, much.'
攵 (a hand with a stick, action) — 数 relates to the action of counting.
娄 (lóu) gives a hint of the sound — 数 is pronounced shù, a connection that has drifted over time.

example.hanzi: 大多数学生都同意这个看法。
example.pinyin: Dàduōshù xuésheng dōu tóngyì zhège kànfǎ.
example.english: The majority of students agree with this view.
example.fact: 大多数 tacks the intensifier 大 ("big, great") onto 多数 ("the greater number, majority") for emphasis — 多数 alone already means "majority," so 大多数 leans closer to "the overwhelming majority," even though both are usually translated into English simply as "most."

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — 速 relates to the speed of movement
束 (shù) gives a loose sound connection to 速's reading sù
广 (a building or shelter) — 度 pictures people gathering indoors.
廿 (twenty) — a group of people meeting to measure or deliberate gave 度 its meaning of a 'degree' or 'measure,' as in temperature or angles.

example.pinyin: Zhè liàng chē de sùdù tài kuài le.
example.english: This car's speed is too fast.
example.fact: 度 by itself already means "a measured degree," as in 温度 ("temperature," literally "warmth degree") — 速度 builds "speed" as literally "the degree of quickness," the same measuring logic behind 湿度 ("humidity") and 高度 ("height, altitude"), a whole family of X度 words naming a quantified degree of X.

components.note: 礻 (an altar, related to ritual/spirits) — 神 relates to gods and spirits.
申 (shēn) gives a hint of the sound — 神 is pronounced shén, a connection that has shifted over time.
纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.

example.pinyin: Tā de shénjīng hěn jǐnzhāng.
example.english: His nerves are very tense.
example.fact: Beyond its anatomical sense, 神经 doubles as an informal insult — calling someone 神经 or 神经病 suggests they're acting unhinged or crazy, similar to how English can call an erratic person "a basket case," extending a medical term into casual slang about someone's mental state.

components.note: 氵 (water) shows 汤 relates to a liquid, as in soup or broth.
昜 (yáng) gives a sound distantly related to tāng, having drifted apart over time.
女 (woman) — 姆 names a woman who cares for children.
母 (mǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 姆's reading mǔ.

example.pinyin: Tāngmǔ shì wǒ de péngyou.
example.english: Tom is my friend.
example.fact: 汤姆 is a phonetic transliteration built purely for sound, not sense — 汤 ("soup") and 姆 (a term for a female caretaker, as in 保姆, "nanny") contribute nothing to the meaning "Tom." Both characters are chosen only because their pronunciations, tāng and mǔ, approximate the English name.

components.note: Ox — animals like oxen were used as sacrifices.
Gives the sound xī, matching the character's reading.
牛 (ox) shows 牲 relates to livestock.
生 (shēng) gives the exact sound of 牲.

example.hanzi: 他为了家人牺牲了自己的事业。
example.pinyin: Tā wèile jiārén xīshēng le zìjǐ de shìyè.
example.english: He sacrificed his own career for his family.
example.fact: 牺牲 originally named the livestock, typically oxen (hence 牛 in both characters), slaughtered in ancient ritual offerings to gods or ancestors — the modern, everyday sense of "to give something up for a greater cause" is a metaphorical extension of that literal ritual sacrifice.

components.note: 力 (strength) — 勇 describes inner strength shown as courage.
甬 (yǒng) is an exact match for the sound of 勇.
耳 — a wild beast being confronted
攵 (a hand with a stick) — striking at the beast, showing boldness

example.pinyin: Xiāofángyuán fēicháng yǒnggǎn.
example.english: Firefighters are extremely brave.
example.fact: 敢 alone already means "to dare" (敢不敢, "dare you or not") — its traditional graphic story shows a hand with a stick confronting a wild beast, a fitting root image for the boldness in the face of danger that 勇敢 names.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 愤 describes a heart filled with anger or resentment.
贲 is only distantly related in sound to fèn — the connection has drifted apart over time.
心 (heart) — 怒 relates to strong feeling in the heart: anger.
奴 (nú) gives a sound close to nù, sharing the same syllable body and differing mainly in tone.

example.hanzi: 他的愤怒完全无法控制。
example.pinyin: Tā de fènnù wánquán wúfǎ kòngzhì.
example.english: His anger was completely uncontrollable.
example.fact: 愤怒 sits at the intense, literary end of Mandarin's anger vocabulary — closer to "wrath, fury" than the everyday, conversational 生气 ("to get angry, annoyed") — so it shows up far more often in writing, news, or formal speech than in casual chat.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with a stick, action) — 数 relates to the action of counting.
娄 (lóu) gives a hint of the sound — 数 is pronounced shù, a connection that has drifted over time.
宀 (a house) — the setting for the scene.
子 (a child) — a child inside the house, perhaps evoking a name being nurtured, the source of 字's meaning 'character, word; courtesy name.'

example.hanzi: 这份报告里有很多数字。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn bàogào lǐ yǒu hěn duō shùzì.
example.english: This report contains a lot of figures.
example.fact: 数字 covers both "a numeral" (a single digit) and, as an adjective, "digital" (数字相机, "digital camera") — the same two characters doing double duty for "number" and "digital" mirrors how English also repurposed "digital" from "relating to digits" into "computerized."

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.pinyin: Yàoshi diào zài dìshang le.
example.english: The keys fell on the ground.
example.fact: 地上 pairs 地 ("earth, ground") with the light, neutral-toned suffix 上 ("on top of") to mean "on the ground/floor" — the same suffix pattern appears in 桌子上 ("on the table") and 床上 ("on the bed"), one of Mandarin's most productive ways to build a location phrase out of any noun.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — the character's original sense connected to a type of plant
氾 (fàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 范's reading fàn
囗 (an enclosure) — 围 relates to surrounding or encircling something
韦 (wéi) gives the sound — 围 is also pronounced wéi, an exact match

example.hanzi: 这个问题超出了我的知识范围。
example.pinyin: Zhège wèntí chāochū le wǒ de zhīshi fànwéi.
example.english: This question is beyond the scope of my knowledge.
example.fact: 围 traces back to 囗, a picture of an enclosure hemming something in on every side; 范围 extends that physical boundary image metaphorically from enclosed space to abstract scope, as in 超出范围 ("beyond the scope") — the same figurative move English makes when it calls an idea's limits its "boundaries."

components.note: 里 (a unit of distance, related to a village measure) — 量 relates to measuring quantity.
旦 (dàn) gives a hint of the sound — 量 is pronounced liàng, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.pinyin: Wǒ huì jǐnliàng zǎo diǎn dào.
example.english: I'll try to arrive as early as possible.
example.fact: 尽量 is easy to confuse with the similarly-spelled 尽力 ("to put in one's full effort/strength"): 尽量 specifically means doing something to the greatest possible extent or quantity (尽量多, "as much as possible"), while 尽力 is about maximum effort, not necessarily maximum amount.

components.note: 太 adds a small dot below 大 (big) — the extra mark emphasizes something even bigger or more extreme, giving 太 its meaning 'too' or 'extremely.'
阝 (a hillside/place) — the sunlit side of a hill or place
日 (the sun) — the source of light and warmth

example.pinyin: Jīntiān de tàiyang hěn dà.
example.english: The sun is really strong today.
example.fact: 阳 names the sunlit side of a hill or place (阝 "hillside" + 日 "sun") and is also half of the yīn-yáng (阴阳) pair representing shade and light. 太阳 tacks on 太 ("very, extremely") for emphasis — literally something like "the extremely bright one."

components.note: 食 (food) — 餐 relates directly to eating and meals.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen yìqǐ chī wǔcān ba.
example.english: Let's have lunch together.
example.fact: 午餐 is the more formal, written-register word for "lunch" — everyday spoken Mandarin reaches far more often for 午饭 (also in this batch), built from the plainer 饭 ("cooked rice, meal"), while 餐 (from 食, "food") carries a slightly more refined tone, as in 早餐/午餐/晚餐 versus the everyday 早饭/午饭/晚饭.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 提 relates to lifting or carrying something by hand.
是 (shì) gives a hint of the sound — 提 is pronounced tí, a connection that has shifted over time.
屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.hanzi: 他在会议上提出了一个新想法。
example.pinyin: Tā zài huìyì shàng tíchū le yí gè xīn xiǎngfǎ.
example.english: He raised a new idea at the meeting.
example.fact: 提出 combines 提 ("to lift, to carry") with the directional complement 出 ("out") to mean literally "to lift out" — a "lift into view" image close to what English does with its own "to raise" a question or proposal, one of the cases where the two languages' metaphors happen to line up.

components.note: 日 (sun, related to time) — 暂 describes a short span of time.
斩 (zhǎn) gives a sound close to zàn.
日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form

example.pinyin: Zhè zhǐshì zànshí de kùnnan.
example.english: This is only a temporary difficulty.
example.fact: 暂时 works as both an adjective ("temporary") and, more commonly, an adverb meaning "for now, for the time being" placed right before a verb (暂时不能, "can't for now") — English needs two different phrases for these two uses, where Mandarin reuses the same word.

components.note: 饣 (food) — 饭 names cooked rice, a meal.
反 (fǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 饭.

example.pinyin: Nǐ wǔfàn chī le shénme?
example.english: What did you have for lunch?
example.fact: 饭 (from 饣 "food" + the sound component 反) literally means "cooked rice" before broadening to "meal" in general — the same shift 饭 makes in 吃饭 ("to eat," literally "to eat rice"), where the specific staple food came to stand for the whole act of eating.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 优 originally described an outstanding performer or actor
尤 (yóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 优's reading yōu
禾 (grain) — 秀 originally described a grain plant coming into flower, extending to 'elegant, outstanding.'

example.pinyin: Tā shì yì míng yōuxiù de lǎoshī.
example.english: She is an outstanding teacher.
example.fact: 秀 alone already means "to flower, to bloom," describing a grain crop coming into flower, and by extension "to excel, to stand out" — 优秀 pairs it with 优 ("superior, excellent") to describe a person or thing that has, so to speak, come into full bloom.

components.note: 木 (tree) — traditionally read as a tree that has borne fruit.
立 (standing) — standing close by to watch it grow, evoking closeness and nurture, extended to 亲's meaning 'close, dear; parent, relative.'
A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'

example.pinyin: Jīnglǐ qīnzì lái dàoqiàn le.
example.english: The manager came to apologize in person.
example.fact: 亲自 emphasizes that someone did something themselves rather than delegating it (亲自来, "came in person," rather than sending someone else) — it pairs the "closeness, intimacy" sense of 亲 with the reflexive 自 ("self"), underscoring direct, hands-on involvement.

components.note: 欠 (breath, an open mouth exhaling) — 歌 relates to the breath used in singing.
哥 (gē) gives the sound — an exact match with 歌's reading gē.
The outline pictures a bent, curved container or musical instrument, giving 曲 its meaning 'crooked, bent' and, by extension, 'a tune.'

example.pinyin: Zhè shǒu gēqǔ hěn hǎotīng.
example.english: This song sounds really nice.
example.fact: 歌 and 曲 are near-synonyms doubled into one word: 歌 emphasizes the sung lyrics (from 欠, a mouth exhaling breath) while 曲 emphasizes the melody or tune, so 歌曲 covers a song as a whole, words and music together — and it takes the measure word 首, as in 一首歌曲.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 婴 names a newborn, closely tied to the mother.
儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.pinyin: Nàge yīngér gāng chūshēng sān tiān.
example.english: That baby was born just three days ago.
example.fact: 婴 (built around 女 "woman," evoking the mother) and 儿 (a pictograph of a small child, drawn with an oversized head) combine into the formal, written-register word for "infant" — everyday spoken Mandarin reaches instead for the plainer, more affectionate 宝宝 ("baby") far more often than 婴儿.
